concepts.name: IAsyncDisposable, await using and async disposal pitfalls
Serializing deployments with GitHub Actions concurrency groups

questions.prompt: A connection class completes pending requests with `tcs.SetResult(response)` from its one socket-reader loop. Under load the reader stalls, because it ends up running the awaiting callers' code. What is the usual fix?

choices.text: Call `TrySetResult` instead of `SetResult`, so the reader no longer waits for the awaiting callers
Create each `TaskCompletionSource` with `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`, so callers get their own thread
Add `ConfigureAwait(false)` inside the reader loop, so continuations stop running on the reader's thread

questions.explanation: By default a task's continuations may run synchronously, inline on the thread that completes it, so `SetResult` can run every awaiting caller's code on the reader thread. `RunContinuationsAsynchronously` makes them dispatch to the thread pool instead. `TrySetResult` only differs in not throwing when the task is already complete, `LongRunning` is a scheduling hint about a task's own work, and `ConfigureAwait(false)` on the reader's own awaits doesn't change where other code's continuations run.

sources.claim: Always create TaskCompletionSource<T> with TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously: by default continuations can run inline on the thread that completes the task, which risks deadlocks and thread-pool starvation; the flag dispatches them to the thread pool.

sources.title: TaskCreationOptions Enum (System.Threading.Tasks)
sources.claim: RunContinuationsAsynchronously forces continuations added to the task to run asynchronously; LongRunning is only a scheduling hint that oversubscription may be warranted; the options can be passed to the TaskCompletionSource<TResult> constructor.

questions.prompt: A library type wraps a network stream and implements only `IAsyncDisposable`, flushing buffered data in `DisposeAsync`. What risk does Microsoft's dispose guidance warn about with this design?

choices.text: Code that disposes it only through `IDisposable` never calls `DisposeAsync`, so it leaks
`await using` refuses to compile for it, since that statement also needs `IDisposable`
The GC calls `DisposeAsync` on the finalizer thread, which can deadlock the whole process
`DisposeAsync` must return a `Task`, so every single disposal allocates on the heap

questions.explanation: If a class implements `IAsyncDisposable` but not `IDisposable`, a consumer that only knows `Dispose` (an older container or wrapper, say) never reaches `DisposeAsync`, and the resource leaks. That's why the guidance suggests implementing both when synchronous disposal is possible. `await using` works with `IAsyncDisposable` alone, the GC never calls `DisposeAsync`, and `DisposeAsync` returns a `ValueTask`.

sources.title: Implement a DisposeAsync method - .NET
sources.claim: If a class implements IAsyncDisposable but not IDisposable and a consumer only calls Dispose, DisposeAsync is never called and resources leak; DisposeAsync returns a ValueTask and is called by await using; stacked await using statements where a later constructor throws leave neither object disposed.

questions.prompt: Two merges to `main` a minute apart both start your GitHub Actions workflow that deploys to production, and the two deploys overlap. How would you use `concurrency` to stop this, and what do its settings do to running and waiting runs?

model_answer.summary: Put the deploy in a concurrency group named for the environment so only one deploy runs at a time; by default a newer waiting run replaces an older one, and `cancel-in-progress` decides whether the running deploy is cancelled.
key_points: A concurrency group allows at most one running job or workflow run at a time; a run that starts while another is in progress waits as pending
By default only one run can be pending: a newer run cancels the older pending one, so intermediate commits are skipped (`queue: max` lets up to 100 wait instead)
`cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the running one, which suits CI on a branch but risks leaving a production deploy half done
Group names are shared by every workflow in the repository, so name them uniquely, for example with `github.workflow` and the environment

questions.explanation: Concurrency groups serialize deploys without any locking in your scripts. The tempting fix is `cancel-in-progress: true` everywhere, but for a production deploy you usually want the running one to finish and only the latest waiting commit to follow it.

sources.title: Control the concurrency of workflows and jobs
sources.claim: A concurrency group has at most one running and, by default, one pending job or run; a newly queued run cancels the existing pending one and takes its place; cancel-in-progress: true cancels the running one; queue: max allows up to 100 pending; group names must be unique across workflows to avoid cancelling other workflows' runs.

questions.prompt: Async guidance from the ASP.NET Core team says to always create `TaskCompletionSource<T>` with `TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously`. Explain what can go wrong without it.

model_answer.summary: Without the flag, completing the task can run the awaiting code inline on the completing thread, which can stall that thread, deadlock it or starve the pool; the flag sends the continuations to the thread pool.
key_points: By default, continuations on the task may run synchronously, on the thread that calls `SetResult`, `SetException` or `SetCanceled`
That thread then runs arbitrary caller code before `SetResult` returns, so a producer loop or timer callback stalls behind it
If the completing code holds a lock or is a scarce thread, inline continuations can cause deadlocks and thread-pool starvation
`RunContinuationsAsynchronously` forces the continuations to be queued to the thread pool, so `SetResult` returns quickly

questions.explanation: A `TaskCompletionSource` is often completed from infrastructure code: a socket reader, a callback, a lock-protected section. Running callers' continuations inline there couples that code to whatever the callers do next.

questions.prompt:
```csharp
var a = new ExampleAsyncDisposable();
var b = new AnotherAsyncDisposable(); // throws
await using (a.ConfigureAwait(false))
await using (b.ConfigureAwait(false)) { }
```

The second constructor throws. What happens to `a`?

choices.text: It is disposed as the exception leaves, because its `await using` is listed first here
It is never disposed, because the throw happens before either `await using` starts
It is disposed by its finalizer at once, as `await using` registered it up front
It is disposed with `b`, because the compiler moves each `await using` above both

questions.explanation: Microsoft's guidance calls this "stacked usings" and says to avoid it: `b`'s constructor throws before execution reaches either `await using`, so `DisposeAsync` is never called on `a`. Nest the blocks, or create each object right before its own `await using`, so every object that was created is disposed.

questions.prompt: A deploy workflow uses `concurrency: production` with the default settings. Run A is deploying and run B is pending when run C is queued. What happens?

choices.text: A is canceled, so that C, the newest run, starts deploying now
B and C both wait in order, and each deploys after the one before
C fails at once, because the group already holds a pending run
B is canceled and C waits as pending; C deploys once A finishes

questions.explanation: A concurrency group has at most one running and, by default, one pending run. A newly queued run cancels the existing pending one and takes its place, so B is skipped and C runs after A. The running deploy is cancelled only with `cancel-in-progress: true`; keeping several waiting runs needs `queue: max`.
